title: Payouts, reserves, and payment cash flow
description: Understand why recorded sales, available provider balance, and money in the bank are three different numbers.
dek: Payment economics include timing. Settlement delays, payout schedules, reserves, refunds, disputes, and FX can matter more than a small rate difference.
takeaways: Gross sales, provider balance, available balance, next payout, and bank cash should be tracked separately.
A payout frequency does not promise that every new transaction is immediately available.
Reserves, negative balances, refunds, disputes, and currency conversion create working-capital needs.

sections.heading: Draw the cash timeline
body: For each payment method, document authorization, capture, settlement, provider availability, payout initiation, and bank arrival. Then add the effect of weekends, holidays, new-account delays, risk reviews, and manual payout schedules.
Do this for normal sales, not only the provider's fastest eligible case. An instant-payout feature is not the same as the default cost and timing of all funds.

sections.heading: Read the balance as a ledger
body: Provider dashboards may separate pending funds, available funds, next payout, reserves, fees, refunds, disputes, and adjustments. A payout is usually a bundle of balance transactions rather than a direct copy of one customer order.
Reconciliation should explain gross collected amount, tax, provider fees, refunds, disputes, currency conversions, reserve movements, and the resulting net payout.

sections.heading: Understand reserves and holds
body: A reserve keeps funds unavailable to cover future refunds, chargebacks, or other exposure. It can be fixed, rolling, transaction-based, or risk-adjusted depending on the agreement. Holds and account limitations can also delay specific payments or broader balances.
Ask what triggers a reserve, how the amount is calculated, when it is reviewed, how release works, and whether the provider can debit a linked bank account to cover a negative balance.

sections.heading: Currencies create separate balances
body: Presentment currency is what the buyer sees and pays. Settlement currency is the currency in which the provider records or converts funds for you. Payout currency is what reaches a bank account. When those differ, conversion timing and fees matter.
Multiple settlement accounts can reduce unnecessary conversions for some providers and countries. They also add reconciliation and treasury complexity.

sections.heading: Model the working-capital buffer
body: Estimate normal payout lag plus a stressed period containing refunds, disputes, provider review, and a reserve. Subscription annual plans and preorders can produce large cash receipts alongside long future service obligations.
Compare providers on predictable net cash and operational resilience, not only headline payment cost. Keep a bank buffer outside the provider balance for payroll, tax, refunds, and continuity.

decisionChecklist: Map settlement and payout timing for every important payment method and currency.
Reconcile provider balance transactions to each bank payout.
Read reserve, hold, negative-balance, and bank-debit clauses.
Model a stressed month with high refunds or delayed payouts.
Keep operating cash outside the payment provider.
